title: Why Pastors Are Leaving Ministry
excerpt: Pastors are not leaving because the work got harder, they are leaving because the work was never the work they were called to, and most of us cannot tell the difference anymore.
body:
A man I trained for the ministry called me last spring to tell me he was done. Not falling, not in scandal, not in doubt about the existence of God. Done. He said the sentence the way a man says it when he has already cleaned out the office and is only calling to be heard once before he stops being a pastor. He had given eleven years to a congregation that loved him and exhausted him in roughly equal measure, and he could not name the thing that broke. That is the part that should frighten us. He could not name it.

I have learned to distrust the easy explanations, because I have used all of them on myself. We say a man left because of conflict, because of money, because his wife was unhappy, because the elders were cruel or the building was failing or the denomination was dying. Sometimes those things are true. But they are rarely the wound. They are the place where an older wound finally tears open. The Barna Group has been tracking this for years, and in their 2021 research forty-two percent of Protestant pastors said they had seriously considered quitting full-time ministry within the previous year (Barna 2021). Two years earlier that number had been considerably lower. Something accelerated. The question is whether we understand what.

The strongest case against my alarm comes from men I respect. They say the exodus is a correction, not a crisis. The men leaving were never built for it, or the culture has simply grown hostile to the faith and is shaking out the casual. There is truth in this, and I will not pretend otherwise. Not every man ordained should have been. Some of us mistook a gift for a call, and a faithful exit is better than a faithless tenure. Eugene Peterson said that the vocation of pastor has been replaced in many men by the profession of running a religious business, and a man can be very good at the business and never have been a pastor at all (Peterson 2011). If those men are leaving, that is not loss. That is honesty.

But that explanation does not account for the men I am actually losing. It does not account for the man who could not name what broke. He was not casual. He was not in it for the platform. He prayed, he visited the dying, he preached texts that cost him. The correction theory works on the periphery and fails at the center, because the men at the center are the ones bleeding out, and they are bleeding out from a wound the theory cannot see.

Let me carry one text through this, because I do not trust my own diagnosis without it. Elijah, after the fire fell on Carmel, after the prophets of Baal were routed, after the single greatest public victory of his ministry, runs into the wilderness and sits down under a broom tree and asks God to kill him. It is enough, he says. Take away my life, for I am no better than my fathers (1 Kings 19:4 ESV). Read that slowly. This is not a man who failed. This is a man who won, and the winning emptied him, and in the emptiness the only prayer he could find was the prayer to die. The text does not treat him as a coward. God does not rebuke him. God feeds him. God lets him sleep. Then God asks him a question, and the question is the whole sermon. What are you doing here, Elijah.

Notice what God does not do. He does not give Elijah a strategy. He does not give him a church growth plan or a five-point recovery framework. He gives him bread, then sleep, then a question, then his own voice in a silence so thin you could miss it. And then, only then, He gives him a successor and a companion, Elisha, because part of what broke Elijah was the lie that he stood alone. I only am left, Elijah says, twice, and both times it is not true. Seven thousand had not bowed. The isolation was a story he told himself, and the story nearly killed him.

I know that story from the inside. There were months in my own ministry when I preached resurrection on Sunday and could not feel my own pulse by Wednesday. I came to faith out of atheism, and one of the strange griefs of conversion was discovering that the church could exhaust the very God it preached, that a man could handle the holy things every day and grow numb to them the way a surgeon grows numb to blood. I was raised without a father, and I think part of why I poured myself into the congregation without limit was that no one had ever taught me a man could be loved without earning it. So I earned. I earned until I was hollow. That is not a confession I enjoy making. It is the truest sentence I can write about why I almost left.

The history here is not ancient, and the dates matter. The modern American pastorate was reshaped in the second half of the twentieth century by the church growth movement, by the rise of the senior pastor as chief executive, by the megachurch model that taught a generation of us to measure faithfulness in attendance and budget. Peter Drucker, the management theorist, became an unlikely patron saint of the large church in the 1980s and 1990s, advising pastors as though the congregation were a firm. Something was gained. Much was lost. We trained men to grow organizations and called it shepherding, and then we wondered why the shepherds were dying of a loneliness no organization can touch. Henri Nouwen saw it early. He left Harvard to live among the disabled at L'Arche precisely because he had become a teacher of intimacy with God who no longer had it (Nouwen 1989). He named the temptation of the minister as the temptation to be relevant, to be spectacular, to be powerful, and he said the way back was downward, toward weakness, toward the place where you are known by God and not by the crowd.

Here is the reversal. The men who are leaving are often the men who took the job most seriously, because the job as we have built it cannot be taken seriously without it eating you. The casual survive. They were never invested enough to be consumed. It is the devoted who burn, because they fed the machine with everything they had, and the machine does not return love. So when we say the strong are surviving and the weak are leaving, we may have it exactly backward. Some of the men leaving are leaving because they were too faithful to a thing that was never worthy of that faithfulness, and they could not separate the unworthy structure from the worthy Lord.

That is where the cross does its work, and it does it as law before it does it as grace. The law first. If your identity is built on the congregation's approval, the congregation is your god, and that god is jealous and cruel and will demand everything and bless nothing. You have broken the first commandment in the holiest-sounding way available to a man. I have. The grace second, and only second. The cross says your worth was settled before you preached a single sermon, settled by a Father who ran toward a son who had earned nothing, settled in blood you did not spill. You cannot be exhausted out of that. The crowd can leave and the building can close and the denomination can die, and the verdict over you holds, because it was never the crowd's verdict to give.

My friend who quit, the one who could not name what broke, called me again months later. He had not gone back to the church. He had gone back to God. The two had become so fused in his mind that losing one felt like losing both, and the great mercy of his leaving was discovering they were never the same. I do not know if he will pastor again. I am not sure that is the question. The question is the one under the broom tree.

We are not losing pastors because the work is hard. We are losing them because we built a work that requires a man to die for a master that is not Christ. Tear that down, and some of them come back. Leave it standing, and we will keep burying the faithful and calling it attrition.

Name the master. Then feed the prophet bread.

### Works Cited

Barna Group. 2021. 38% of U.S. Pastors Have Thought About Quitting Full-Time Ministry in the Past Year. Ventura, CA: Barna Group.

Nouwen, Henri J. M. 1989. In the Name of Jesus: Reflections on Christian Leadership. New York: Crossroad.

Peterson, Eugene H. 2011. The Pastor: A Memoir. New York: HarperOne.

The Holy Bible, English Standard Version. 2001. Wheaton, IL: Crossway.

title: Depression in the Pulpit: A Pastor's Mental Health
excerpt: The man who tells your congregation that there is hope can sit in his study on Saturday night unable to find any for himself, and the church has built a theology that makes him hide it.
body:
I have preached a sermon on the goodness of God on a morning when I could not feel it. I want to begin there, because I am tired of articles about pastoral depression written as though the writer observed it from a clean distance. I did not observe it. I stood in a pulpit with my chest full of lead and told three hundred people about a joy I was, in that hour, unable to locate in myself. Some of you reading this know exactly the weight I mean. You have done it too. We do not talk about it, and the not talking is part of the sickness.

There is a sentence pastors learn to say without believing it. I am fine. We say it in the narthex with a smile that took years to perfect. We say it to elders who would panic if we said anything else. We say it to our wives until our wives stop believing us and start grieving in silence beside us. The smile is a skill, and like every skill it can be practiced until it runs without the soul behind it. A man can be the most fluent liar in his own life, and the lie he tells best is the one about his own condition.

The strongest objection to taking this seriously is theological, and it comes from sincere men, so I will give it its full weight. They say depression in a believer, and especially in a shepherd, is finally a failure of faith. The joy of the Lord is your strength. Rejoice in the Lord always. If a man truly believed the gospel he preaches, the argument goes, he would not be crushed, and to treat his despair as a medical condition is to excuse a spiritual one. I understand the instinct. There is a kind of modern therapy culture that dissolves all sin into syndrome, that lets a man off every hook by renaming every failure a wound. That culture is real and it is wrong, and I will not defend it.

But the argument fails on its own ground, because it cannot survive contact with the Bible it claims to honor. The Psalms are full of men of profound faith in profound despair. Why are you cast down, O my soul, the psalmist asks himself, and the very next breath he is still cast down (Psalm 42:5 ESV). Jeremiah curses the day he was born. Job, whom God Himself calls blameless, longs for death across thirty chapters. And there, again, is Elijah under the broom tree, a man who had just called down fire from heaven, asking God to take his life (1 Kings 19:4 ESV). If despair were always faithlessness, then the most faithful men in Scripture were the most faithless, and that is an absurdity the argument cannot escape. The God of the Bible does not treat Elijah's collapse as sin to be rebuked. He treats it as a body and a soul to be fed.

Let me carry Elijah through, because his story is the truest map I know for this. Read what God does. He does not preach to Elijah. He sends an angel who bakes bread and touches him and says, twice, arise and eat (1 Kings 19:5-7). The first prescription for the despairing prophet is food and sleep. Let that land on the men who think the cure for a depressed pastor is more Scripture memory and a sterner devotional life. Sometimes the holiest thing a crushed man can do is eat a meal and sleep through the night. The body is not a distraction from the soul. The body is where the soul lives, and a body that has not slept in three weeks will lie to a man about God, about hope, about whether the morning is worth rising for.

Then, after the bread and the sleep, God brings Elijah to the mountain and is not in the wind, not in the earthquake, not in the fire, but in a sound of thin silence (1 Kings 19:11-12). I find that almost unbearable in its tenderness. The God who answered Baal's prophets with fire answers His broken servant with quiet. He does not shout at a man who is already on the floor. We could learn to pastor each other that way. We could learn to pastor ourselves that way.

I said I would be inside this and not above it, so here is the inside. There was a winter in my ministry when I sat in my study every Saturday night and could not finish the sermon, not because the text was hard but because I could not assemble a reason to care. I am a man who came to faith out of atheism, and the cruelty of that season was the return of the old silence, the suspicion that the universe was empty after all, arriving now in the very office where I prepared to preach it full. I was raised without a father, and I had spent my life proving I could carry things alone, and depression is the bill that comes due for a man who has never let anyone carry him. I told no one for far too long. I am a pastor. I am supposed to be the one who carries. The pride of that is its own confession.

The history of how the church got here is worth naming, because shame this specific is usually manufactured. For much of the modern era the church inherited a folk theology that read all suffering as either punishment or insufficient faith, and the holiness movements and parts of the revival tradition sharpened it. Then the twentieth century added the cult of the victorious Christian life, the smiling-pastor-as-brand, the platform that punishes any visible weakness with declining attention. Charles Spurgeon, who knew this country well, preached through depression so heavy he sometimes could not leave his bed, and he told his students plainly that fits of depression come over the most of us, that the strong are not always vigorous, the wise not always ready, the brave not always courageous, and the joyous not always happy (Spurgeon 1875). The man Victorian England called the prince of preachers was describing his own broom tree. We forgot him, and built a culture that would have shamed him into silence.

The research confirms what the silence hides. Lifeway Research found that nearly a quarter of pastors have personally struggled with some kind of mental illness, and about half of those said the illness had been diagnosed (Lifeway 2014). A quarter. Look out across the men at your next denominational gathering and do the arithmetic, then remember that the number is almost certainly low, because the instrument was a survey, and pastors have a trained reflex for telling surveys that we are fine.

Here is the reversal that the smiling theology cannot hold. The pastor's despair is not always his disqualification. It is sometimes the very ground of his usefulness, because a man who has been to the floor and found God still there preaches resurrection with a weight that the untouched cannot fake. Henri Nouwen called this the wounded healer, the minister whose own wounds become a source of healing for others, not when they are hidden but when they are made available (Nouwen 1972). The point is not to perform the wound. The point is that a man who has suffered and been met by God in it can sit with a suffering parishioner and not flinch, because he has been in that room and knows the way the light eventually comes in.

Now the cross, and the law before the grace. The law first. If you are hiding your despair to protect your reputation, your reputation has become your idol, and you are willing to drown privately rather than let the body of Christ see that you bleed. That is not humility. That is pride wearing humility's coat, and I have worn it. The grace second. The cross is the place where God Himself entered the dark and cried out that He was forsaken, and that cry means there is no basement of human despair where Christ has not already been. My God, my God, why have you forsaken me (Matthew 27:46 ESV). The man in the pulpit who feels forsaken is not outside the gospel. He is standing exactly where the gospel happened. The Savior went into the silence so that the silence would never again be the final word over a single one of His shepherds.

So tell someone. Not the congregation from the platform, necessarily, but someone. A brother, a physician, a counselor, a friend who will bake the bread and not preach the sermon. The God who fed Elijah is not ashamed of your weakness. The only one ashamed of it is you, and that shame is a liar.

The pulpit is not a place you have to be well to enter. It is a place a wounded man tells the truth about a God who meets the wounded. Be that man. Then go eat something and sleep.

### Works Cited

Lifeway Research. 2014. Study of Acute Mental Illness and Christian Faith. Nashville: Lifeway Research.

Nouwen, Henri J. M. 1972. The Wounded Healer: Ministry in Contemporary Society. New York: Doubleday.

Spurgeon, Charles H. 1875. Lectures to My Students. London: Passmore and Alabaster.

The Holy Bible, English Standard Version. 2001. Wheaton, IL: Crossway.

title: How to Lead Without Losing Your Soul
excerpt: A man can gain a thriving church and lose the very soul that was supposed to lead it, and most of the practices we call leadership are how he does it.
body:
Jesus asked a question once that every ambitious pastor should have tattooed somewhere he reads it daily. What does it profit a man to gain the whole world and forfeit his soul (Mark 8:36 ESV). He was not speaking to stockbrokers. He was speaking to disciples, to men who wanted to be great, and the warning lands hardest on those of us whose whole world is the work of God. A pastor can forfeit his soul building a kingdom and call the forfeiture sacrifice.

I have watched it happen, and I have felt it happening in myself, which is the only reason I am allowed to write about it. There is a way of leading a church that slowly hollows out the man leading it, and the tragedy is that it often looks like success from the outside. The attendance climbs. The staff grows. The man is busy, sought after, effective. And inside, the well that fed all of it is running dry, and he is preaching from memory of a God he used to know rather than communion with the God he has.

Let me steel-man the resistance, because there is a real and good objection to a whole genre of writing about pastoral self-tending. The objection says that ministry is meant to cost. The shepherd lays down his life for the sheep. Paul poured himself out as a drink offering and counted it joy. There is a modern obsession with the leader's wellness that can become a thin gospel of comfort, a way of dressing up self-protection as wisdom, and a pastor who is forever guarding his peace will never go to the hospital at two in the morning, never absorb the abuse a flock sometimes inflicts on the one who loves them. Sacrifice is not the disease. Sacrifice is the calling. I believe that, and I will not retreat from it.

But the objection mistakes the thing being protected. The argument I am making is not that a pastor should spend himself less. It is that he must be filled from a source that the spending cannot empty, or the spending becomes suicide rather than sacrifice. There is a difference between a candle and a battery. A candle gives light by consuming itself, and when it is gone it is gone. The pastor is not called to be a candle. He is called to be a branch on a vine, abiding, drawing life from a root, giving fruit precisely because he himself is being fed. Cut the branch off and tell it to bear fruit through sheer sacrificial will, and you get a dead stick that produces nothing and calls its barrenness devotion.

So I will carry one text, the vine, through this whole piece. Abide in me, and I in you. As the branch cannot bear fruit by itself, unless it abides in the vine, neither can you, unless you abide in me (John 15:4 ESV). Read the next line, the one we skip. Apart from me you can do nothing (John 15:5). Nothing. Not less. Nothing. Jesus did not say apart from Him we can do a reduced amount of slightly weaker ministry. He said the works of a disconnected branch amount to zero, no matter how impressive the branch looks while it withers. The most frightening possibility in pastoral ministry is a man building something large and fruitless, a great visible nothing, because he severed himself from the vine in order to have more time to produce fruit.

I know the severing intimately. I came to faith out of atheism, and converts often carry a fear that the whole thing depends on their effort, because they remember a time when there was no grace holding them and they survived on will alone. I was raised without a father, so I learned early that love had to be earned and that rest was for men who could afford it. Put those two facts in a pastor and you get a machine. For years I treated abiding as a luxury I would get to once the work was under control, which is to say never, because the work is never under control. I was a branch trying to manufacture sap. I produced a great deal of activity and was, in the years I am least proud of, doing nothing.

The history of how we got here has a shape worth tracing. The modern leadership-pastor is a relatively recent invention. Through the twentieth century, and especially from the 1970s forward, the American church absorbed the language and the instincts of corporate management. The pastor became the visionary, the leader, the CEO of a religious enterprise, and the seminaries followed, adding leadership tracks and strategic planning to curricula that once taught prayer and the cure of souls. Eugene Peterson watched this happen and named it as a betrayal of the office. He said pastors had become a company of shopkeepers, and the shops they kept were churches, busy with the trivia of religious commerce, asking how to keep the customers happy, how to lure customers away from competitors, how to package the goods (Peterson 1987). The work of attending to God in the depths got crowded out by the work of running the store. And a man can run a very good store and lose his soul behind the counter.

I want to press on the word abide, because it is the verb the whole vine passage turns on, and it is the verb we are worst at. To abide is not to visit. A man does not abide in a place he stops by between appointments. He abides where he lives, where he returns at the end of every day, where his deepest sense of home is located. Jesus is describing a continuous dwelling, a settled communion that does not switch off when the sermon is finished and the office locks. And the test of whether a man is abiding is not how he performs on Sunday. The test is what happens in his soul on the ordinary Thursday when nothing is required of him, whether his instinct is to run back to the vine or to run to the next task. I have failed that test for whole seasons of my ministry, abiding in the work and merely visiting the Lord, and the fruit of those seasons looked alive on the branch and was already dying at the stem.

There is a cost to admitting this in front of other pastors, and the cost is the very thing that keeps us silent. We are supposed to be the men who have figured out the life with God, who teach others to abide. To confess that we ourselves have been severed branches running on stored sap feels like disqualification. It is not. Bonhoeffer, writing for a community of pastors under pressure, insisted that the man who cannot be alone with God should beware of community, and the man who cannot bear community should beware of being alone, that the two are bound together and a failure in one corrupts the other (Bonhoeffer 1954). The pastor who has no interior solitude with God brings only his anxious, performing self into the life of the church, and the church feels it, even when it cannot name it.

Here is the reversal, and it cuts against everything the leadership industry sells. The most useful thing a pastor does for his people is often the thing that produces nothing visible at all. The hour of prayer that fills no seats. The day of rest that the calendar resents. Edwin Friedman, a rabbi and family therapist, argued that the single most important variable in a leader's effectiveness is not technique but the leader's own differentiated, non-anxious presence, his capacity to stay connected to people while not being absorbed and driven by their anxiety (Friedman 1999). A pastor who has not tended his own interior life becomes a tuning fork for every fear in the congregation, vibrating with the room, unable to lead because he has no ground to lead from. The interior work is not retreat from leadership. It is the precondition of leadership that does not destroy the leader.

Now the cross, law first. The law exposes the lie under the workaholism, and the lie is this. You do not actually believe the work is God's. If you believed God builds the house, you would be able to sleep while He builds it, and your inability to rest is a sermon you are preaching to yourself every day about who you really think is in charge. Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labor in vain (Psalm 127:1 ESV). The verse goes on to say He gives to his beloved sleep. Your insomnia is a doctrine. I have preached that false doctrine to myself for years, and it is a denial of the gospel dressed as diligence.

The grace second. The cross means the decisive work is already finished, accomplished by Another, signed in blood you did not spill. It is finished, He said, and He meant it, and your frantic addition to a completed work is not piety, it is unbelief (John 19:30 ESV). The gospel frees a man to labor hard precisely because his identity does not ride on the labor. He can pour himself out at the hospital bed at two in the morning and then sleep without guilt, because the sleep is not laziness, it is faith that the vine keeps feeding the branch while the branch rests.

The soul is not a resource you spend on the church. It is the place where you meet the God who sends you to the church, and if you spend it, you have nothing left to send.

Guard the root. Let the fruit take care of itself.

### Works Cited

Bonhoeffer, Dietrich. 1954. Life Together. Translated by John W. Doberstein. New York: Harper and Row.

Friedman, Edwin H. 1999. A Failure of Nerve: Leadership in the Age of the Quick Fix. New York: Seabury Books.

Peterson, Eugene H. 1987. Working the Angles: The Shape of Pastoral Integrity. Grand Rapids: Eerdmans.

The Holy Bible, English Standard Version. 2001. Wheaton, IL: Crossway.

title: The Interior Life of the Pastor
excerpt: A pastor can handle the things of God all week and starve to death spiritually, because handling is not the same as eating.
body:
There is a particular kind of hunger that only afflicts people who work with food all day. The cook surrounded by meals he never sits down to eat. The pastor surrounded by Scripture he only ever prepares for someone else. I have stood in my study with an open Bible at ten on a Tuesday morning and realized, with a cold clarity, that I had not read a word of it for my own soul in weeks. I had read it for the sermon. I had read it for the funeral. I had not read it for the bread it is. That is a confession, and it is more common among us than we admit.

The interior life is the part of a pastor that no one sees and everything depends on. It is the man as he is when the building is empty, when no one is watching the prayer, when there is no sermon to harvest from the text. And it is precisely because no one sees it that it is the first thing to go. We are paid for the public man. We are evaluated on the public man. The interior man pays no bills and fills no pews, and so he gets fed last, which means in a busy season he does not get fed at all.

Let me grant the strongest objection before I go further, because it has weight. Some will say this whole emphasis on the pastor's inner world is a modern indulgence, a kind of spiritual navel-gazing that the apostles would not have recognized. Paul did not write about his interior life. He planted churches, took beatings, ran hard, and trusted God to sustain him in the running. The fixation on inner experience, the objection goes, is a symptom of a therapeutic age that has turned even prayer into a project of self-improvement, and a pastor would do better to obey God and stop monitoring his own soul like a man taking his temperature every hour.

There is truth there, and I want to honor it. A spirituality that is forever examining itself can curdle into a new kind of self-absorption, and the cure for an anxious pastor is not always more introspection. But the objection misreads its own apostle. Paul wrote that though our outer self is wasting away, our inner self is being renewed day by day (2 Corinthians 4:16 ESV). He had an interior life, and he tended it, and the running he did was fueled by a renewal that happened in the hidden man. The objection also forgets the Lord Himself, who, in the press of a ministry more urgent than any of ours, rose while it was still dark and went out to a desolate place and prayed (Mark 1:35). The most needed man in Israel withdrew from the need to be with His Father. If He required it, the notion that we have outgrown it is not maturity. It is presumption.

So I will carry that text, Mark 1, through this. The scene is exact and it indicts me. Jesus has healed all evening, the whole town gathered at the door, and the next morning, very early, while it is still dark, He gets up and goes off alone to pray. Then the disciples find Him, almost scandalized, and say everyone is looking for you (Mark 1:37). There is the pressure every pastor knows. Everyone is looking for you. The work is waiting. The needs are stacking up at the door. And the Son of God had, the night before, chosen the desolate place over the waiting crowd, not because the crowd did not matter but because He could not be for the crowd what He needed to be without first being alone with the Father. He drew His public ministry out of His hidden communion. We try to run a public ministry on an empty interior, and then wonder at the hollowness in our own preaching.

I come at this as a man who began with no interior life at all that he would have called by that name. I was an atheist. The inner world I had was a closed room with no window toward heaven, and the great surprise of conversion was the window opening. But here is the danger I did not anticipate. A man can be converted and then slowly board that window back up, not with unbelief but with busyness, until the room is once again sealed, and the strange agony of a sealed-up Christian is that he remembers the light and cannot find it. I was raised without a father, and prayer, the practice of being a beloved child before a present Father, was the very muscle I had never developed and most needed. For years I prayed the way a stranger speaks to a landlord. It took a long time to learn to pray the way a son speaks to a father who is glad he came in.

The history of how pastors lost the interior life is partly a history of good intentions. The Protestant recovery of the Word rightly put preaching at the center, but over centuries the pastor's relationship to Scripture quietly shifted from the man who feeds on it to the man who processes it. Ruth Haley Barton describes the way leaders come to relate to spiritual things functionally, using prayer and Scripture as tools for ministry rather than as means of their own communion with God, until they are, in her phrase, leading on empty (Barton 2008). Dallas Willard spent his life arguing that the missing piece in evangelical ministry was a real apprenticeship to Jesus in the actual practices of the inner life, that we had reduced the gospel to a transaction about the afterlife and lost the present reality of life with God (Willard 1998). We trained men to explain the bread. We did not always teach them to eat it.

Here is the reversal. The hidden life is not preparation for the real work. The hidden life is the real work, and the public ministry is its overflow. Eugene Peterson said the three pastoral acts of praying, reading Scripture, and giving spiritual direction are so unobtrusive that they are easy to skip, and yet they are the angles, the unseen lines, that determine whether the visible shape of the ministry is true or distorted (Peterson 1987). Skip the angles, and the visible structure looks fine for a while, then slowly goes crooked, and everyone can see the crookedness but no one can name the cause, because the cause is invisible. The cause is a man who stopped meeting God in private and is now performing a God he no longer knows.

There is a practical objection I should answer before I reach the cross, because busy men will raise it. When. When does a pastor whose week is already full of urgent need find the hours for a hidden life that produces nothing the church can see. I have asked it myself, usually in the tone of a man looking for permission to skip the thing he knows he needs. But notice that the question assumes the interior life is one more task to be fit into a full schedule, and that assumption is the disease. The interior life is not an item on the list. It is the soil out of which everything else on the list either grows healthy or grows sick. A farmer does not ask when he will find time to have soil. The soil is the precondition of the harvest, and the man who neglects it to spend more hours planting is not more diligent, he is farming dust. Jesus rose before dawn not because His calendar had a gap but because His public life was unsustainable without His hidden one, and so is yours, and so is mine.

There is also a quieter reason we avoid the interior life, and it is worth naming because naming it is half the cure. The hidden room is where God deals with us about ourselves, and many of us would rather stay busy than be that exposed. As long as I am preparing a sermon I am safe, I am the one with the answers, I am the handler of the text and not its subject. The moment I sit in the dark before dawn with nothing to prepare and no one to instruct, the text turns and begins to read me, and what it finds is not always flattering. Avoidance of the interior life is often avoidance of self-knowledge before God, and a pastor can hide from his own soul behind the very Scriptures he expounds. I have done it. The flight into busyness can be, underneath, a flight from the God who wants to tell me the truth about myself, and that truth is the doorway to every mercy I most need.

The cross, law first. The law here is sharp. To handle the holy things professionally while not communing with the Holy One personally is the sin of the man who serves at the altar and despises the One the altar is for. It is possible to preach Christ and not know Christ, to be, in the end, a tour guide pointing at a country he has never entered. I have stood closer to that man than I want to say. The grace second. The cross opened the way into the very presence of God, tore the veil from top to bottom, made the holiest place accessible to a man with bloody hands and a divided heart (Matthew 27:51). The invitation to commune is not earned by the quality of your interior life. It is purchased by Christ and offered to you in your emptiness. You do not have to assemble a worthy inner life before you come in. You come in empty, and the coming in is how it fills.

The pastor's most important sermon is the one no one will ever hear, preached in a dark room before dawn, to an audience of One.

Feed the hidden man. The visible one is starving in front of you.

### Works Cited

Barton, Ruth Haley. 2008. Strengthening the Soul of Your Leadership: Seeking God in the Crucible of Ministry. Downers Grove, IL: InterVarsity Press.

Peterson, Eugene H. 1987. Working the Angles: The Shape of Pastoral Integrity. Grand Rapids: Eerdmans.

Willard, Dallas. 1998. The Divine Conspiracy: Rediscovering Our Hidden Life in God. San Francisco: HarperSanFrancisco.

The Holy Bible, English Standard Version. 2001. Wheaton, IL: Crossway.

title: Why Your Church Should Require a Sabbatical
excerpt: A church that will not let its pastor rest has already decided it values his output over his soul, and it should not be surprised when the output one day stops.
body:
Most churches will let a pastor work himself into the ground and call it dedication. The same church that would never ask a member to work without a single sustained rest for a decade will ask exactly that of the man who shepherds them, and it will frame the asking as a compliment. We need you. We could not do it without you. That sentence has buried more pastors than scandal ever has, and the congregations that spoke it stood at the graveside genuinely confused about what went wrong.

I want to make a practical argument with a theological spine. Churches should not merely permit sabbaticals. They should require them, structurally, in writing, the way a wise company requires a pilot to rest before he flies you across an ocean. A permitted sabbatical that a driven pastor is free to decline will be declined, because the kind of man who most needs the rest is precisely the kind who will refuse it to prove he does not. The rest must be mandated, or the men who need it most will martyr themselves to avoid it. I am that kind of man. I know whereof I speak.

Let me give the objection its full weight, because it is sincere and it is widespread. A small church will say, plainly, that it cannot afford this. We have one pastor. There is no staff to cover. The bills do not pause because the shepherd is tired, and a three-month absence could mean a collapse in giving, in attendance, in momentum a small congregation cannot recover. There is also a theological version. Some will say the New Testament knows nothing of pastoral sabbaticals, that Paul never took one, that this is a borrowed academic perk dressed up in spiritual language, an entitlement the apostles would not recognize. These are not foolish objections. They come from people who love their churches and fear for them.

I will answer the practical fear honestly. Yes, it costs something. So does a funeral, and so does the search for a replacement, and so does the slow decline of a congregation led for ten years by a man running on fumes who has stopped, without anyone noticing, actually meeting God. The expensive thing is not the sabbatical. The expensive thing is the burned-out pastor you keep on the field because resting him felt unaffordable, who is now doing visible nothing while appearing to do everything. A church can find pulpit supply for three months. A church cannot so easily replace fifteen years of trust when the man holding it finally breaks.

Now the theological objection, which I take more seriously, and here I will carry one text through the whole argument. The objection says Scripture does not command pastoral rest. But Scripture commands rest at the level of creation itself, woven into the order of things before there was ever a church to manage. On the seventh day God finished his work that he had done, and he rested on the seventh day from all his work that he had done. So God blessed the seventh day and made it holy (Genesis 2:2-3 ESV). Read what is happening. The God who does not tire chose to rest, and chose to bless and sanctify the rest, not because He needed it but because He was establishing a rhythm into the fabric of the world that His creatures would need to the depths of their being. The Sabbath was not given to Israel as a suggestion. It was the fourth commandment, set among prohibitions of idolatry and murder, and the reason given is creation itself (Exodus 20:8-11). A pastor who will not rest is not being more spiritual than his Creator. He is quietly claiming to be stronger than the God who stopped.

I break this commandment more easily than the others, and so do you, and we feel righteous doing it. No one praises a man for committing adultery. Congregations applaud a man for never taking a day off. The sin that gets applauded is the hardest sin to repent of, because the applause keeps telling you it is a virtue. I came to faith out of atheism, and I came in with the instincts of a man who believed everything depended on his own effort, because for the years before grace it had. I was raised without a father, and rest, in my body, has always felt like the thing you do not get to have until the work is done and the work is never done. So I worked through Sabbaths and called it love for the church, and what it actually was, underneath, was a refusal to trust that God could run His church for one day without me. That is not humility. That is a small and exhausting blasphemy.

The history here is instructive, because the church once knew this and forgot it. The Sabbath principle shaped Western life for centuries, and the academic sabbatical, which churches now eye with suspicion as a worldly luxury, was itself derived from the biblical sabbatical year, the seventh year in which the land of Israel was commanded to lie fallow so the soil would not be exhausted (Leviticus 25:4). The world borrowed the idea from Scripture, kept it, and now the church looks at its own ancient practice as though it were an intrusion from outside. Zack Eswine, writing to weary pastors, names the lie underneath our refusal to rest, the belief that we must be a kind of god for our people, everywhere for everyone, fixing everything, immune to limits, and he says the recovery of pastoral health begins with the humbling and freeing admission that we are not Christ, that we have a body, that we are creatures and not the Creator (Eswine 2015). Refusing to rest is, at bottom, refusing to be a creature.

I should say plainly what a required sabbatical is and is not, because the word frightens small churches who picture a man on a beach for a season while the bills pile up. It is not a vacation, though it should contain real rest. It is not a sabbatical in the academic sense of producing a book, though some men will write. It is a fallow season, a deliberate lying-down of the soil, in which a pastor steps back from the relentless demand of being available in order to be filled again from the only source that fills. The shape can be modest. Even a smaller church can build toward a month of true absence after every few years, with the elders covering pulpit and care, and that month, guarded and required, can do more for the long health of a ministry than another year of unbroken grinding ever will. The size of the church does not change the law of the Sabbath. It only changes the creativity required to obey it.

The elders carry a particular weight here, and most of them have never been told. A pastor who is the kind of man who needs rest most will not ask for it, because asking feels like confessing weakness to the very people who evaluate him. So the request must not be his to make. The structure must make the rest automatic, removed from his discretion, the way a good father takes the car keys from a son too proud to admit he is too tired to drive. Edwin Friedman observed that anxious systems pressure their leaders into chronic overfunctioning, that the more responsible a leader is, the more the system will lean on him until he breaks (Friedman 1999). A church can love its pastor straight into the ground without ever intending harm, simply by leaning, and leaning, and never once telling him to stop. The mandate to rest is how a wise body stops leaning on the man it cannot afford to lose.

Here is the reversal. The pastor who never rests is not serving the church most. He is teaching it, week after week, by the sermon of his own unbroken availability, that a human being is what holds the church together, and that is the most dangerous lesson a congregation can learn. When he finally falls, and the church discovers it survives without him, the discovery is brutal precisely because he taught them it was impossible. A pastor who rests, who lets the church run for a season without him, preaches a truer gospel by his absence than many preach by their presence, because his absence says out loud what his frantic presence denied. Christ holds this church. Not me.

The cross, law first. The law exposes the idol, and the idol is the pastor's own indispensability, which is a sweeter and more spiritual-sounding idol than money or sex and therefore harder to smash. To believe the church cannot survive your rest is to believe you are its head, and the church has only one head, and it is not you, and that headship was settled at a cross where you were not even conscious, where the decisive work was done by Another while you contributed nothing but the sin He carried. The grace second. The same cross that dethrones you frees you, because if Christ holds the church then you may, at last, put it down and sleep. There remains a Sabbath rest for the people of God, the writer of Hebrews says, for whoever has entered God's rest has also rested from his works as God did from his (Hebrews 4:9-10 ESV). The gospel is not a summons to work harder for God. It is, in the end, an invitation to stop, because the work that saves the world is finished, and the man who cannot stop has not yet believed it.

So write the sabbatical into the bylaws. Require it. Make rest a law in your church before exhaustion makes a casualty of your pastor.

A church that cannot let its shepherd rest has not yet learned who the Shepherd is.

### Works Cited

Eswine, Zack. 2015. The Imperfect Pastor: Discovering Joy in Our Limitations through a Daily Apprenticeship with Jesus. Wheaton, IL: Crossway.

Friedman, Edwin H. 1999. A Failure of Nerve: Leadership in the Age of the Quick Fix. New York: Seabury Books.

The Holy Bible, English Standard Version. 2001. Wheaton, IL: Crossway.
